CONTEXT.content: As apps grow, mixing HTTP handling, business logic, and database access in one file becomes unmaintainable. Layered architecture separates concerns so each piece can be tested, changed, and debugged independently.
CONTEXT.analogy: A restaurant has distinct roles: waiter (handles requests), chef (business logic), pantry (data storage). You wouldn't want the waiter cooking or the chef taking orders.
CONTEXT.productionNote: Teams that skip layering early pay 10x in refactoring when the app reaches production scale.
hints: Look at your current code — where are three different concerns mixed together?

DECIDE.optionA: Monolith with clear internal layers: routes → service → repository.
DECIDE.optionB: Keep it flat for now but define interfaces so layers can be extracted later.

tradeoffs.A: More files upfront; easier testing and debugging immediately.
tradeoffs.B: Faster now; extraction cost grows with codebase size.

hints: Consider how painful the BREAK step will be with each choice.

BUILD.goal: Refactor your URL shortener into three layers: handler (HTTP), service (business logic), repository (database).

tracks.node: Separate into routes/, services/, repositories/ directories.

acceptance: Service layer works without HTTP (testable in isolation)
Repository handles all SQL — no queries in handlers
Errors in DB layer return 500, not unhandled crashes
hints: Start by identifying what each layer should NOT know about.
The service should not know about HTTP status codes.
The handler should not know about SQL.

criteria: Show a test or script calling the service directly (no HTTP)
Show error handling: DB failure returns 500 with safe message
Explain which layer owns each piece of logic
hints: Can you test business logic without starting the web server?

BREAK.scenario: After deploy, some requests return 500 with 'internal error' but logs show the real error is being swallowed.
BREAK.symptoms: Happy path works. Invalid input returns 400 correctly. Database timeout returns generic 500 with no useful log.
hints: Which layer is responsible for logging?
Is an error being caught and re-thrown without context?

FIX.goal: Fix error propagation so failures are logged with context but clients see safe messages.
hints: Errors should gain context as they bubble up, not lose it.
The handler decides what the client sees; inner layers decide what gets logged.

decisionCallbacks.A: Your layers made the error-swallowing bug easier to locate — you knew exactly which layer should have logged.
decisionCallbacks.B: The flat structure made it harder to know where error handling should live, which is why the bug hid.
